job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting and Loophole Review

**Highest-impact items for Thursday:** #1 (single-vessel threshold), #11 (no ban on processing, sale, or import), #15 (environmental assessment exemption), #20 (effective-date conflict), and #28 (sunset conflict).

## Scope and Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator can split production across several vessels that each stay below it and avoid coverage.

2. **§2(1)(A), volume measurement:** The bill doesn't say whether the 10,000 metric tons refers to wet or dry weight, or to tonnage recovered versus shipped, and it doesn't aggregate production across affiliated companies.

3. **§2(1)(A), "polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources":** "Mineral resources" is undefined, leaving unclear whether cobalt crusts, polymetallic sulfides, or other seabed deposits are covered, and how their volume is measured.

4. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's discretion:** The Secretary can extend the definition to any activity judged "comparable" in ecosystem risk, but the bill sets no standard, process, or notice requirement, and "comparable" and "deep-sea ecosystems" are undefined. This is vulnerable to arbitrary-and-capricious and vagueness challenges.

5. **§2 and §3(a), core terms undefined:** "Commercial," "recovery," "mining," and "engage in" are not defined. It is unclear whether exploration, test collection, processing, transport, and pilot production count as covered activity.

6. **§2 and §6, "Secretary":** §2(1)(B) uses "the Secretary" without specifying which Secretary, while §6 names the Secretary of State. The enforcing agency for the discretionary authority is unclear.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** Limiting this to citizens and state-organized corporations excludes LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, which are common operating vehicles. A Delaware LLC running operations would not be a "U.S. person" under §3(a)'s second clause.

8. **§2(3), "vessel" and "equipped for":** Neither term is defined, so it's unclear whether unmanned collectors, towed systems, barges, or support ships count.

9. **§2(3) and §4, 5,000-gross-ton threshold:** "Covered vessel" appears only in the registry provision and not in the prohibition. Smaller recovery vessels fall outside registration and reporting entirely.

10. **§3(a), territorial reach:** "In the United States" is not defined to include the EEZ or continental shelf, and the bill doesn't address activity in the Area beyond national jurisdiction. Foreign-flagged vessels and foreign persons abroad are reached only through the "U.S. person anywhere" clause.

11. **§3(a), prohibits mining only:** The bill doesn't ban processing, sale, import, financing, insurance, or procurement of nodule-derived metals. A company could stop recovery within U.S. reach while continuing to trade or process ore from other sources.

## Exemptions and Grandfathering

12. **§3(b), "mining conducted under an exploration license":** Exploration licenses authorize exploration, not commercial recovery. Read literally, the exemption could cover commercial-scale recovery conducted under an exploration license.

13. **§3(b), no limits on grandfathered activity:** The exemption doesn't restrict renewal, extension, transfer, expansion, or production increases, and it has no end date.

14. **§3(b), undefined licensing terms:** "Exploration license" is undefined, and the bill doesn't cross-reference the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, which as I understand it separately authorizes commercial recovery permits. Whether those permits are covered is unclear, and the policy team should confirm the statutory references with counsel.

15. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** There is no volume cap, approval requirement, reporting obligation, or time limit, and "purpose" is subjective. Commercial-scale recovery could be relabeled as assessment activity.

## Registry and Reporting

16. **§4(a), registration:** The bill sets no deadline or required content for registration, and "operator" is undefined. It doesn't say which party registers when ownership and operation are held by different entities.

17. **§4(b), reporting content:** "Describing the recovery activities" doesn't specify tonnage, location, depth, or disposition of recovered material. It also sets no deadline, verification, or public-access requirement.

18. **§4 and §5, no enforcement for registry failures:** Penalties attach only to violations of §3, so failure to register or file reports carries no penalty. False certifications would be reachable only under general federal statutes, not under this Act.

## Penalties and Enforcement

19. **§5(a) and §8, effective-date conflict:** §5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the prohibition's effect by 180 days. A court could read the penalty provision either way, and this invites a challenge.

20. **§5(a), "each day" and no minimum penalty:** "Each day" is undefined for continuing violations at sea, and because the penalty is a ceiling only, nominal penalties are permissible and can be treated as a cost of doing business.

21. **§5, no enforcement machinery:** The bill names no enforcing agency and no procedure (administrative or judicial). It also gives no investigative authority, injunctive relief, or citizen-suit provision.

22. **§5, no asset remedies:** There is no forfeiture or seizure of vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals, and no port-access or federal-funding restrictions. Penalties alone may not deter operators with large resources.

23. **§5(b), "willfully":** The term is undefined, so the criminal provision is open to vagueness challenges and to disputes over corporate-officer liability.

24. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The Act "shall cease to have effect" after 10 years, without preserving pending enforcement actions or accrued penalties.

25. **General drafting, no severability, preemption, or relationship to existing law:** The bill doesn't address severability, doesn't say whether it supersedes the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, and doesn't amend or repeal that statute. A court could find an implied conflict with existing permitting authority, which gives opponents an argument.

## Timing and Duration

26. **§8, 180-day window:** Commercial recovery stays lawful until the effective date, and nothing prevents companies from ramping up production or stockpiling during that period.

27. **§7(a) and §7(b), internal conflict:** §7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is passed, while §7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. A court would likely treat the sunset as controlling, so the prohibition could lapse at year 10 regardless of any National Academies report.

28. **§7(a), "serious harm," NAS report, and joint resolution:** "Serious harm" is undefined. The bill sets no deadline, scope, or funding for the National Academies report and no expedited procedure for the joint resolution. It is also unclear whether a congressional "finding" has operative legal effect.

29. **§6, "seek to negotiate":** The Secretary of State is required only to seek negotiations, not to conclude an agreement, and no consequence follows if talks fail. "Equivalent" is undefined, and the bill doesn't reference the International Seabed Authority or the status of the United States under UNCLOS.

---

**Notes for the policy team:**

- Items 14, 25, and 28 involve statutory interplay and constitutional questions. Please have counsel confirm the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act references and any challenge theories before they go into testimony.
- Some of these points, such as the ambiguities and enforcement gaps, can be raised in testimony. Others, such as the exemption and grandfathering points, could prompt sponsors to tighten the language, which may hurt us. Decide in advance which points to press publicly and which to raise privately with staff.
